title: Tuning snare and bass drums for the street and the dance band
summary: Rene explains loosening the snare for the sun, a vibrating bass drum and tuning the bass drum to a key.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used

blocks.x: But, uh... Well, let's see, I was going to ask you about tuning your drums in the street. How would you tune your snare drum?

Well, now, the snare drum, you had to tune the snare drum loose. Couldn't truly try a drum. I'll tell you the reason why you had to do that, on account of the sun. You had to keep, you know, your snare drum with... I hear some bass drums sound awful on the street, man. Sound like you're hitting on a piece of wood that's dead, you know? Don't care. Sometimes the drums be too tight, I'd loosen it up. You see a...you notice the bass drum on a parade, if it got a vibration, it cares more, it sounds more nicer. I always did like a drum with a solid little vibration, where it carries, you know? It's more effective, don't you think so? Oh yeah. Accent sound, you know?
Well, they have some dead drum ones, none of them.

Yeah. I mean, this is sort of a bad, you know? As long as he's playing in time, you don't care how it sounds. But I think if a drum is tuned up real nice, it almost inhomens the band, you see? Most of them are sort of a tipply effect, you see? That gives them a nice sound. Because I know I used to chew my drum and then sometimes I'd, if we had a lot of numbers and like in G and D and stuff like that, I'd chew my bass drum to G. And then it sounds right along with the band.
You mean that's in the dance band?
